1992). The drainage area of the Lahn River at the down-
stream end of the study reach is approximately 2700 km
2.
Floodplain soils, which consist of A/AC/C profiles, are
developed in silty loam sediments deposited during the
last 1000 years. In valleys elsewhere in Germany, aggrada-
tion during this time has been attributed to clearing of
hillslopes, which disturbed soils and increased sediment
delivery to channels (Huckriede 1971; Schirmer 1983;
Thiemeyer 1988). In most of the study reach, this late
Holocene sediment reaches a thickness of up to 2 m; in
some proximal floodplain positions, however, it is over-
lain by an additional 1–3 m of sandy silt deposited since
the late-seventeenth century (Mäckel 1969). Similar to
most rivers in Germany, the Lahn River was channelized
in the mid-nineteenth century, and since then has main-
tained virtually the same channel position. A survey of
aerial photography from 1935 to 1995 revealed no lateral
channel migration in the study reach during the last 60
years. Floods in the Lahn River drainage typically occur
during the winter and early spring. Such events inundate
most of the floodplain, but, as corroborated by field ob-
servations of flooding during the winter of 1995, they de-
posit little sediment on distal floodplain positions. Most
sedimentation occurs immediately adjacent to the chan-
nel.
In this study, six heavy metals (Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Pb, and
Zn) that typically show evidence of anthropogenic enrich-
ment were investigated. Concentrations in floodplain sur-
face soils were measured at five cross-sections located be-
tween Wetzlar and Marburg (Fig. 1). To determine
whether valley width has affected sediment storage (Mag-
illigan 1985), and therefore metal contents, samples were
collected from three narrow-valley (Roth, Sichertshausen,
Dorlar) and two wide-valley reaches (Garbenheim, Heu-
chelheim). Sites were located the maximum distance pos-
sible from obvious sources of heavy metals (e.g., major
roadways, industrial concentrations). At each site, sam-
ples of approximately 100 g were taken from the upper
5 cm of surface soils and placed in sterile plastic bags.
The interval between samples across the floodplain
ranged from 25 m to 100 m, depending on floodplain
width.
Fig. 1
Location of Lahn River study reach between Marburg and
Wetzlar, Germany. Study sites are: D Dorlar; G Garbenheim; H
Heuchelheim; R Roth; S Sichertshausen
In order to assess the possible anthropogenic input of
metals, pre-industrial metal levels (hereafter referred to
as background metal values) were calculated for the
study area (see Förstner and Müller 1981; de Groot and
others 1982). Commonly, background metal values are
derived from pre-industrial sediments or from the exten-
sion of worldwide average metal values (e.g., Turekian
and Wedepohl 1961) to a given geographical region. Al-
though worldwide average metal values are often applied
to specific drainage basins, pre-industrial sediments, be-
cause they are obtained from the same location as sam-
ples analyzed for heavy metal content, would appear to
provide the most accurate values for pre-industrial metal
levels of a drainage system.

Commonly, background metal values are
derived from pre-industrial sediments or from the exten-
sion of worldwide average metal values (e.g., Turekian
and Wedepohl 1961) to a given geographical region. Al-
though worldwide average metal values are often applied
to specific drainage basins, pre-industrial sediments, be-
cause they are obtained from the same location as sam-
ples analyzed for heavy metal content, would appear to
provide the most accurate values for pre-industrial metal
levels of a drainage system. Using a soil auger, eight
background samples were obtained from a depth of at
least 1 m. Care was taken to retain only the internal part
of a sample that had not come in contact with the auger
barrel. Samples were stored in sterile plastic bags and
transported to the laboratory.
Following the method used by many researchers (e.g., Sa-
lomons and Förstner 1980; de Groot and others 1982;
Ntekim and others 1993; Mantei and Sappington 1994),
heavy metal concentrations were measured for only silt-
size and smaller fractions ( ~0.063 mm). Particles of this
size typically contain the bulk of heavy metals. Samples
were first sieved to remove the Á2 mm fraction. Splits
for particle size analysis and organic matter determina-
tion were then separated. Additional sieving removed the
Á0.063 mm fraction. From the remaining ~0.063 mm
fraction, approximately 40 g of sediment were removed

and stored in plastic bags for heavy metal analysis. Sam-
ples were first digested with percholoric, nitric, and hy-
drofluoric acids. The residue was then taken up in a vol-
ume of 10% hydrochloric acid. For the measurement of
Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, and Zn levels, the solution was analyzed
by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectros-
copy (ICP-AES); Pb concentrations were determined by
atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS). Results, which are
corrected for spectral interelement interferences, are re-
ported in ppm.
In addition to the heavy metal analysis, particle size and
organic matter analyses were completed on all samples.
Particle size distribution of clay and silt was determined
following the pipette method (Köhn 1929). Sand fractions
were separated by wet sieving. Because sediment texture
often affects metal contents (Förstner and Müller 1981;
Macklin and Dowsett 1989; Mantei and Sappington 1994),
trends in particle size distribution and metal contents
were compared across sample sites. Likewise, organic
matter content, also an important determinant of metal
concentrations (Salomons and Förstner 1984; Leenaers
and others 1988), was derived by loss-on-ignition at
430 7C for 24 h (Davies 1974).
Results and discussion
Tables 1 and 2 list the mean metal concentrations for the
study reach as a whole and individually for each site.
Background metal values are also provided. As Table 2
indicates, the Heuchelheim background metal values dif-
fer markedly from background values of the other four
sites. Their effect on the mean background metal values
is evident when they are excluded from calculations (Ta-
ble 1). Although the high metal contents of the Heuchel-
heim background samples are similar to levels found in
post-1800 sediments, radiocarbon ages indicate that the
samples date to the pre-industrial period. The Heuchel-
heim background samples were collected at depths of
1.5 m and 1.75 m from a black, organic-rich peat. Subse-
quently, uncalibrated radiocarbon ages on the peat of
1620B70 years BP (Utc-4124) at a depth of 1.5 m and
1950B70 years BP (Utc-4123) at a depth of 1.75 m were
obtained (A. Stobbe, Unpub. data). The ages demonstrate
that the background samples were collected from sedi-
ments deposited at least 1600 years ago.

__data__.text:
Although the high metal contents of the Heuchel-
heim background samples are similar to levels found in
post-1800 sediments, radiocarbon ages indicate that the
samples date to the pre-industrial period. The Heuchel-
heim background samples were collected at depths of
1.5 m and 1.75 m from a black, organic-rich peat. Subse-
quently, uncalibrated radiocarbon ages on the peat of
1620B70 years BP (Utc-4124) at a depth of 1.5 m and
1950B70 years BP (Utc-4123) at a depth of 1.75 m were
obtained (A. Stobbe, Unpub. data). The ages demonstrate
that the background samples were collected from sedi-
ments deposited at least 1600 years ago. Additionally, the
ages indicate that the collection of samples for heavy me-
tal background values at a depth of 1 m, as was done in
this research, likely ensured that only pre-industrial sedi-
ments were sampled. The anomalously high metal con-
tents of the Heuchelheim background samples may stem
from high organic (10%) and clay contents (61%). The
high clay and organic contents are suggestive of accumu-
lation in a backwater setting, which may have served as a
sink for metals being conveyed through the Lahn drai-
nage basin. An alternative explanation for the high metal
contents of the samples is that they may have a different
source area than do the samples from which the other
background values were measured. Because the back-
ground values from the other four sites are approximate-
ly equal, they are considered representative of pre-indus-
trial metal concentrations in sediments of the study
reach, and therefore are used in assessing the anthropo-
genic contribution of metals.
Comparison of the mean surface metal contents with
background values indicates that floodplain soils are con-
taminated with Cu, Pb, and Zn, but not with Cd, Co, and
Cr (Table 1). The mean level of Cu for the 50 samples is
1.5 times the background level (excluding Heuchelheim),
the levels of Pb and Zn are approximately twice the back-
ground level. According to contamination standards de-
veloped for the Lahn River on the basis of the Geoaccu-
mulation Index (Muller 1979), floodplain soils are moder-
ately contaminated with Pb and Zn, but only lightly con-
taminated with Cu (Die Lahn, Ein Fliessgewässerökosy-
stem 1994). The metal levels in floodplain soils are also
lower than the mean concentration for Cu (75 ppm), Pb
(105 ppm), and Zn (409 ppm) measured in bed sediments
(~2 mm) of the Lahn River by Knoblich and Sanner

As indicated in Table 2, there is only minor site-to-site
variation in floodplain metal contents. Apparently, valley
width has little effect on metal concentrations in flood-
plain soils; narrow valley sites (Roth, Sichertshausen,
Dorlar) have virtually the same metal contents as do
wide-valley sites (Heuchelheim, Garbenheim). Only at the
Garbenheim site are the values slightly higher, possibly
because of the proximity of the site to a downstream
steel mill, metal scrapyard, and busy four-lane highway.
These may contribute metal-contaminated aerosols to the
floodplain. Because no major tributary enters the Lahn
River between the Dorlar and Garbenheim sites, the addi-
tion of materials from a different source area does not
appear to explain the higher metal contents.

As indicated in Table 2, there is only minor site-to-site
variation in floodplain metal contents. Apparently, valley
width has little effect on metal concentrations in flood-
plain soils; narrow valley sites (Roth, Sichertshausen,
Dorlar) have virtually the same metal contents as do
wide-valley sites (Heuchelheim, Garbenheim). Only at the
Garbenheim site are the values slightly higher, possibly
because of the proximity of the site to a downstream
steel mill, metal scrapyard, and busy four-lane highway.
These may contribute metal-contaminated aerosols to the
floodplain. Because no major tributary enters the Lahn
River between the Dorlar and Garbenheim sites, the addi-
tion of materials from a different source area does not
appear to explain the higher metal contents.
In order to look at the distribution of metals across the
floodplain, transects depicting Cu, Pb, and Zn contents,
percentage of silt and clay, and organic matter content
for the Dorlar and Garbenheim sites were compiled (Figs.
2 and 3); the other sites have similar trends. Only the
heavy metals that show evidence of anthropogenic en-
richment are portrayed. At both sites the heavy metal
concentrations, especially that of Zn, are high adjacent to
the active channel, but drop sharply within a distance of
approximately 25 m from the channel bank. The high
contents near the channel bank do not appear to result
from a relatively high percentage of fine sediment or high
organic matter content as sample points having higher
organic matter contents and great percentages of fine se-
diment, but lower metal contents, are found elsewhere on
the floodplain. The probable explanation for the high
concentrations near the channel is that this position of
the floodplain is inundated most frequently, thereby re-
ceiving regular inputs of sediments and metals. Because
the Lahn River is contaminated more with Zn than with
Cu or Pb, the decline in Zn concentration across the
floodplain is proportionally greater with distance from
the channel than is the decline in Cu and Pb. The sites
not depicted in Figs. 2 and 3 show a similar decrease in
Cu, Pb, and Zn concentrations with increasing distance
from the river.

metal concentrations, organic matter content, and per-

centages of silt and clay vary little. Excluding near-chan-
nel positions, floodplain zones having anomalously high
metal concentrations, which have been noted in other
drainage basins (e.g., Wolfenden and Lewin 1977; Bradley
and Cox 1990; Dehner 1994), are not present in the study
reach. This suggests that when flooding occurs, most se-
diment and metals are deposited close to the active chan-
nel; other parts of the floodplain apparently receive
roughly equal, but lesser, quantities of sediments and
metals. The absence of any metal sinks can probably be
explained by the minimal topography of the floodplain.
Topographic lows (e.g., old channels) that would favor
the deposition of metalliferous fine sediment are rare in
the study reach. Additionally, the Lahn River has mean-
dered little, if at all, since channelization in the mid-
1800s. Consequently, there are few abandoned channels
filled with post-nineteenth century metal-rich alluvium.
The metal concentrations of Lahn River floodplain soils
are much lower than concentrations measured in surface
soils of major drainage basins elsewhere in Germany. For
example, Cu, Pb, and Zn concentrations in the study
reach are substantially lower than the mean Cu
(206 ppm), Pb (123 ppm) and Zn (1190 ppm) concentra-
tions of floodplain soils along the Elbe River, one of the
most polluted rivers in Europe (Brügmann 1995). Similar-
ly, metal concentrations in Lahn floodplain soils are less
than the mean values for Cu (32 ppm), Pb (73 ppm) and
Zn (232 ppm) measured in floodplain soils of the Rhine
River in west-central Germany (Dehner 1994). Notwith-
standing these differences, the results from this study in-
dicate that the Lahn River has received anthropogenic in-
puts of heavy metals. The decline in metal contents with

distance from the active channel suggests that most me-
tals reached the floodplain via fluvial rather than eolian
deposition. Although metal concentrations are low-to-
moderate, floodplain surface soils should be regarded as
a potential source for future heavy metal pollution. Final-
ly, it is worth noting that several recent studies in Ger-
many demonstrate that surface soils often have lower
heavy metal contents than do subsurface sediments
(Müller 1988; Dehner 1994; Brügmann 1995). The differ-
ence is attributed to reduction in metal releases to the
environment over the last 20–30 years. If such is the case
in the Lahn River drainage basin, then higher stores of
metals may be present in and just below the lower A ho-
rizon of modern floodplain soils.
Conclusions
Accurate prediction of future heavy metal loads in large
European river systems can emerge only when the levels
of heavy metals stored in major tributary valleys are
known. In aggregate, tributaries have the potential to
serve as important future sources of heavy metal pollu-
tion. To this end, heavy metal contents in floodplain soils
were measured for a 60-km reach of the Lahn River, a
major tributary to the Rhine River. Samples were found
to contain low-to-moderate levels of heavy metals. In
comparison to the metal contents of pre-industrial sedi-
ments collected from the subsurface, surface soils at five
sites are slightly contaminated with Cu and moderately
contaminated with Pb and Zn; concentrations of Cd, Co,
and Cr in surface soils are nearly identical to concentra-
tions in pre-industrial sediments. Virtually no site-to-site
variation in metal concentrations was discernible, sug-
gesting that valley width has had no effect on the concen-
tration of metals in surface soils. At each site, floodplain
metal concentrations are highest immediately adjacent to
the active channel. Metal contents drop sharply with in-
creasing distance from the river and are essentially uni-
form across the floodplain. Metal sinks, or areas of the
floodplain with anomalously high metal concentrations,
were not identified in the study reach. Additionally, no
clear relationship among particle size distribution, or-
ganic matter content, and metal concentrations could be
established.
In comparison with other rivers in Germany (e.g., Rhine,
Elbe), the level of metal contamination in the Lahn River
basin is relatively low. Nevertheless, this research demon-
strates that drainage basins distant from major industrial
concentrations have received inputs of anthropogenic
heavy metals. Because the high levels of contamination
are at and immediately adjacent to the Lahn River, the
bulk of these metalliferous sediments would appear to be
fluvial rather than eolian deposits. Although presently
immobile under the channelized hydrological condition
of the river, these metals could be eroded if the hydro-
logic regime became more energetic, especially if it were
characterized by lateral channel migration. Should this
occur, the metals would likely be transported through the
narrow downstream reach of the Lahn River, where
stream power is proportionally higher, potentially reach-
ing the Rhine River.

Persistence of trace metal contamination in a fluvial system: Lahn River, 
central Germany 
Charles W. Martin 
Department of Geography and Geospatial Sciences, 1002 Seaton Hall, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506-2904, USA   
ARTICLE INFO  
Keywords: 
Trace metals in the environment 
Floodplain sediment contamination 
Monitoring of trace metals 
German rivers 
ABSTRACT  
To monitor short-term changes in trace metal concentrations (Cu, Pb, Zn) at geomorphically sensitive floodplain 
locations and examine the persistence of contaminants in the fluvial environment, near-channel sites along the 
Lahn River, central Germany, that were sampled in 2007 were revisited in 2019. Thirty-three cores were 
extracted from sites < 5 m from the active channel along a 75-km reach of the river. The median concentrations of 
Cu and Zn in 2019 were statistically unchanged from concentrations in 2007, but median concentrations of Pb in 
2019 were statistically higher than in 2007. Concentration of all three trace metals remain above the background 
concentrations, but only Zn concentrations exceed the 2 ϭ background upper limit. On an individual sample site 
basis, the Cu concentration increased at 48 % of the sites and the Zn concentration increased at 45 % of the sites 
between 2007 and 2019. Pb concentration increased at 70 % of the sites. Concentrations of trace metals generally 
increased with distance downstream; the lowermost reach of the Lahn River continues to have the highest 
concentration of trace metals. Between 2007 and 2019, the concentrations (mean and median) of all three metals 
increased in the uppermost and lowermost sections of the study area whereas in the middle section the mean and 
median concentrations of Cu and Zn and the median concentration of Pb decreased (the mean concentration of 
Pb increased in the middle reach). Changes in metal concentrations between 2007 and 2019 do not appear to be 
caused by factors such as changes in substrate of samples, variable sedimentation rates and flood history, or the 
percentage of clay and organic matter content. Elevated concentrations of trace metals persist in near-channel 
sediments and will continue to pose a risk of future downstream heavy metal pollution in the study reach, 
especially along the lowermost reach of the Lahn River where the most contaminated sediments are located. 
Trace metal concentrations in the study reach appear to have become “ uncoupled ” from overall decreases in 
metal releases to the environment.   
1. Introduction 
Many river systems throughout Europe reflect the legacy of long- 
term exposure to pollutants, including trace metals. Often the product 
of industrial activity or mining, trace metals have in some locations been 
released to European rivers for centuries ( Matschullat et al., 1997 ; 
Br ¨annvall et al., 1999 ; Bindler et al., 2011 ; Kincey et al., 2018 ; Wang 
et al., 2019 ). The release of trace metals to the environment was at a 
maximum from the early- to mid-nineteenth century until the early 
1970s and has decreased since then ( Renberg et al., 2001 ; Middelkoop, 
2002 ; Ciszewski and Grygar, 2016 ; Dhivert et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 
2019 ). Historical events in Europe since the late 1980s and growing 
awareness of the dangers of trace metals in the environment have 
resulted in cleaner rivers and floodplain sediments across much of 
western Europe ( Brügmann, 1995 ; Middelkoop, 2002 ; Zerling et al., 
2006 ; Martin, 2015 ; Wang et al., 2019 ). Technological advances in 
water treatment plants and industrial facilities in eastern Europe further 
reduced the spread of air and water pollution in Europe ( Scherer et al., 
2003 ; Zerling et al., 2006 ). 
In Germany, surface waters have become markedly cleaner over the 
last few decades ( Wang et al., 2019 ), but high concentrations of trace 
metals remain along many rivers.

Historical events in Europe since the late 1980s and growing 
awareness of the dangers of trace metals in the environment have 
resulted in cleaner rivers and floodplain sediments across much of 
western Europe ( Brügmann, 1995 ; Middelkoop, 2002 ; Zerling et al., 
2006 ; Martin, 2015 ; Wang et al., 2019 ). Technological advances in 
water treatment plants and industrial facilities in eastern Europe further 
reduced the spread of air and water pollution in Europe ( Scherer et al., 
2003 ; Zerling et al., 2006 ). 
In Germany, surface waters have become markedly cleaner over the 
last few decades ( Wang et al., 2019 ), but high concentrations of trace 
metals remain along many rivers. Metals are often stored in channel 
banks and near-channel sediments, geomorphically sensitive areas 
where sediments and attached pollutants are easily eroded ( James, 
1989 ; F ¨orstner, 2003 ; Foulds et al., 2014 ; Clement et al., 2017 ). Sedi -
ment samples collected shortly after major flood events have established 
that high concentrations of trace metals may be transported by high 
discharges and subsequently deposited in downstream floodplains 
( F ¨orstner, 2003 ; Krüger et al., 2005 ; Schwartz et al., 2006 ; Foulds et al., 
2014 ; Le Gall et al., 2018 ). Although the release of trace metals to the

Geomorphology 426 (2023) 108603
2
environment is less today than in the past, trace metals stored in 
floodplain sediments, named legacy sediments by James (2013) , should 
be regarded as future sources of trace metal pollution ( Schwartz et al., 
2006 ; Ciszewski and Turner, 2009 ; Dennis et al., 2009 ; Foulds et al., 
2014 ; Wadige et al., 2016 ; Esser et al., 2020 ). 
Urbanized, industrial, or mined watersheds, which typically 
generate the highest releases of trace metals to the environment, have 
been the focus of numerous studies over the last two decades (e.g., 
Middelkoop, 2002 ; Macklin et al., 2006 ; Ciszewski and Turner, 2009 ; 
Dennis et al., 2009 ; Resongles et al., 2014 ; Ilie et al., 2017 ; Matache 
et al., 2018 ; Szab ´o et al., 2020 ). Much of this work documents anthro -
pogenic enrichment of trace metals along rivers downstream from ur -
banized, industrial, or mined areas in which floodplain trace metal 
concentrations exceed background concentrations, or values that reflect 
non-anthropogenic metal concentrations ( Birch et al., 2000 ; Matschullat 
et al., 2000 ; Bindler et al., 2011 ; 
ˇ
Strbac et al., 2018 ; Geiselbrecht et al., 
2019 ). Less is known about trace metal storage in non-urbanized, non- 
industrial areas, or non-mined areas (an exception is Murad and Fischer, 
1978 ). 
The Lahn River basin is a relatively agrarian watershed with a 
drainage area of ~5000 km
2
. Trace metals are clustered in near-channel 
positions of the floodplain ( < 5 m from active channel), with lower 
concentrations present with distance from the near-channel zone 
( Martin, 2009 ). The concentration of trace metals (Cu, Pb, Zn) along the 
Lahn River is less than that noted along waterways such as the Rhine or 
Elbe, although individual sites have metal concentrations approaching 
levels associated with urbanized, industrial, or mined watersheds 
( Martin, 2004 ). Trace metal concentrations are higher along the Dill 
River, a tributary to the lower Lahn River, and the lower Lahn River 
itself; both the Dill River and lower Lahn River have a history of up -
stream industrial activity and mining ( Martin, 2015 ), although mining 
appears to be less important than industrial activity in contributing trace 
metals to the watersheds ( Martin, 2019 ). Vertically, surface samples 
collected at numerous sites along the Lahn and Dill rivers generally 
contain lower concentrations of trace metals than do samples collected 
at greater depths ( Martin, 2015 ), a reflection of continuing declines in 
metal releases to the environment that has been documented elsewhere 
(e.g., Middelkoop, 2002 ; Zerling et al., 2006 ; Le Gall et al., 2018 ; 
Buchty-Lemke et al., 2019 ). 
The present study extends previous research on changes in heavy 
metal concentrations at channel bank locations along a 75-km reach of 
the Lahn River between Marburg and Weilburg, documented in Martin 
(2004, 2012) , and explores the persistence of trace metals in the 
floodplain environment. Near-channel locations sampled in 2000 and 
2007 were revisited and resampled in 2019 to evaluate the persistence 
of trace metals along the Lahn River. Specific objectives of the study are 
to (i) determine changes since 2007 in trace metal concentrations in the 
upper 5 cm of floodplain soils at near-channel ( < 5 m from active 
channel) locations sampled in 2007, (ii) examine changes between 2007 
and 2019 along the upper vs. lower reaches of the Lahn River, (iii) assess 
continued contributions of the Dill River to trace metals concentrations 
along the lower Lahn River, and (iv) assess the conveyance of trace 
metals during a flood through sampling of flood sediments deposited in 
March 2019 along a reach of the upper Lahn River.

__data__.text:
Near-channel locations sampled in 2000 and 
2007 were revisited and resampled in 2019 to evaluate the persistence 
of trace metals along the Lahn River. Specific objectives of the study are 
to (i) determine changes since 2007 in trace metal concentrations in the 
upper 5 cm of floodplain soils at near-channel ( < 5 m from active 
channel) locations sampled in 2007, (ii) examine changes between 2007 
and 2019 along the upper vs. lower reaches of the Lahn River, (iii) assess 
continued contributions of the Dill River to trace metals concentrations 
along the lower Lahn River, and (iv) assess the conveyance of trace 
metals during a flood through sampling of flood sediments deposited in 
March 2019 along a reach of the upper Lahn River. This study extends 
my work on short-term changes in the concentrations of heavy metals 
and allows evaluation of the persistence of metal storage in channel 
bank sediments of the Lahn River. Channel bank positions are relatively 
active geomorphically and regarded as potentially significant sources for 
future heavy metal pollution ( James, 1989 ; Marcus, 1989 ; Leigh, 1997 ; 
Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2001 ). Finally, this work presents an opportunity 
to assess whether declines over the last several decades in trace metal 
releases to the environment are reflected in trace metal concentrations 
at near-channel positions along the Lahn River, or whether there is a lag 
in the response of metal concentrations in the floodplain to declines in 
metal releases to the environment. 
2. Study area 
Starting in the uplands north of Marburg, the Lahn River drains 
about 5000 km
2 
of predominantly rural landscapes ( Fig. 1 ). In the 75-km 
long study reach between Marburg and Weilburg, the Lahn valley is 
broad, reaching a maximum width of 2.5 km just downriver of Giessen. 
Urban centers of Marburg, Giessen, and Wetzlar, with most industrial 
activity concentrated in Wetzlar, contrast with the rural and agrarian 
land use elsewhere in the basin. Nearly three-quarters of land in the 
drainage basin is classified as agriculture with lesser amounts of forested 
land (16 %) and urban land (14 %), according to J ¨ockel (1981) . Personal 
observation from nearly 25 years of working in the study reach indicate 
little or no land-use change along the floodplain and uplands over the 
study period. Uplands are typically forested and floodplains are culti -
vated or grazed. Channel bank riparian vegetation consists of scattered 
deciduous trees and a ~ 3-m-wide near-channel vegetation zone 
composed of low-lying brush. Cultivation, where present, generally does 
not extend to the channel bank. Near-channel surface soils have a mean 
pH of 5.2 (standard deviation 0.5), a clayey-silt texture (60 % silt and 
clay, clay content 15 – 20 %), and organic matter content of ~10 %. 
Large-scale mining in the Lahn River watershed is not documented be -
tween Marburg and Wetzlar, but there is a history of iron mining during 
the late nineteenth century and much of the twentieth century in close 
proximity to the Lahn River between Wetzlar and Weilburg ( Meyer, 
2007 ). Iron ore was mined during the same period along the Dill River, 
which empties into the Lahn at Wetzlar. The last iron mine in the study 
area closed in the early 1980s. 
The Lahn River was extensively modified through deepening and 
channelization beginning in the mid-nineteenth century. As part of the 
modifications, many small step-dams were built, which have the effect 
of reducing flow velocity and stream power. The channel gradient along 
the Lahn River is low, generally between 0.02
◦
and 0.14
◦
. Although it is 
generally a quiet, tranquil river, flooding and overbank flow do occur, 
typically between January and April. The high flows are generated by 
late winter and early spring precipitation and early spring snowmelt in 
upland areas.

Iron ore was mined during the same period along the Dill River, 
which empties into the Lahn at Wetzlar. The last iron mine in the study 
area closed in the early 1980s. 
The Lahn River was extensively modified through deepening and 
channelization beginning in the mid-nineteenth century. As part of the 
modifications, many small step-dams were built, which have the effect 
of reducing flow velocity and stream power. The channel gradient along 
the Lahn River is low, generally between 0.02
◦
and 0.14
◦
. Although it is 
generally a quiet, tranquil river, flooding and overbank flow do occur, 
typically between January and April. The high flows are generated by 
late winter and early spring precipitation and early spring snowmelt in 
upland areas. Overbank flows have the capacity to erode channel banks 
and deposit fine sediments on point bars and near-channel surfaces as 
was the case in March 2019 during the field work for this study. A series 
of aerial photographs taken between 1935 and 1995 and personal field 
experience in the study reach suggest that the Lahn River channel has 
been stable for at least several decades. Meander swales scattered across 
the floodplain in the study reach provide evidence that lateral channel 
migration has occurred in the study reach, likely prior to mid-1800s 
channelization. 
3. Methods 
Locating the 33 sites where channel bank sediments were collected in 
2000 and 2007 involved using GPS coordinates contained in field notes, 
topographic maps, and ground-based photographs ( Fig. 1 ). As was the 
case in 2000 and 2007, sample sites are positioned < 5 m from the active 
river channel. I used an Oakfield handheld corer at each sample site to 
collect a 2.5 cm diameter core from the floodplain. The upper 5 cm of 
each core was sampled and placed in sterile plastic Whirlpack bags for 
transport to the geomorphology lab at Justus Liebig-Universit ¨at, Gies -
sen. As was done in 2007, the latitude and longitude of each sample site 
was recorded using a handheld GPS unit. Standard sediment analyses 
were done on one half of each sample in the geomorphology lab. Grain 
size analysis involved determination of the proportions of clay ( < 2 μ m) 
and silt (2 – 63 μ m) using the pipette method and sand percentage 
through wet sieving. Organic matter content was measured by loss on 
ignition (LOI) at 430 
◦
C for 24 h ( Davies, 1974 ). 
The other half of each sample was submitted to ALS Chemex Labs (an 
ISO 9002 registered analytical laboratory in North America) for analysis 
of trace metals. Samples were submitted to the same ALS Chemex lab 
facility in North Vancouver, BC, Canada, that I have used in my previous 
C.W. Martin

Geomorphology 426 (2023) 108603
3
work along the Lahn River and identical laboratory preparation pro -
cedures were followed (air drying of samples, screening to 63 μ m). The 
< 63 μ m fraction size from each sample was digested in perchloric, nitric, 
and hydrofluoric acids (triple-acid digestion). Based on work by Lecce 
and Pavlowsky (1997) , this process yields near total recovery of metals. 
Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscope (ICP-AMS) 
was used to measure concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn, with an analytical 
sensitivity of 1.0 mg kg 
� 1 
for Cu and 2.0 mg kg 
� 1 
for Pb and Zn. Co -
efficients of variation on repeated measurements of standards, as sup -
plied by quality control data from ALS Chemex, were 2.8 % for Cu, 3.5 % 
for Pb, and 2.6 % for Zn. Analysis of duplicates produced a mean dif -
ference of 1.1 mg kg 
� 1 
for Cu, 2.1 mg kg 
� 1 
for Pb, and 8.8 mg kg 
� 1 
for 
Zn. 
To control for substrate influence on metal concentrations, concen -
trations were normalized by dividing them by Al and Fe concentrations 
and clay and organic matter (OM) content (all reported in %). 
Normalizing to “ conservative ” elements such as Al and Fe is a commonly 
used technique to detect anthropogenic metal contributions. Early de -
scriptions of this technique are found in Salomons and F ¨orstner (1984) , 
Schropp et al. (1990) , and Horowitz (1991) , and it continues to be used 
in a variety of geomorphic settings (e.g., Loring, 1991 ; Ho et al., 2012 ). 
Grain size and organic matter content have also been shown to influence 
metal concentrations ( Horowitz, 1991 ; Owens et al., 2005 ), whereas 
others find no correlation between metal concentrations and organic 
matter or fine sediment contents ( Lokas et al., 2010 ). Near-channel al -
luvium along the Lahn River typically has a clayey-silt texture (~60 % 
clay and silt), with clay contents around 15 – 20 %. The organic matter 
content of surface sediments is typically 10 % ( Martin, 2009 ). 
Thirty-five background samples, which are assumed to represent the 
pre-industrial age (pre-1750 A.D.) metal concentrations, were collected 
at various locations along the study reach of the Lahn River at depths of 
0.85 to 1.15 m. They serve as the basis for measuring the magnitude of 
anthropogenic heavy metal enrichment in surface soils. Background 
samples were collected at channel bank sites where surface samples 
were collected ( n = 18 ) and at sites in the study reach that were < 10 m 
from the Lahn River channel ( n = 17 ). Background samples could not be 
collected at all surface sample sites because gravel layers or a high water 
table prevented coring to depths sufficient to reach pre-industrial age 
sediments. The trace metal concentrations in background samples were 
determined by ALS Chemex (North Vancouver facility) with the same 
procedures used for analyzing surface samples. The determination of 
natural background, or nonanthropogenic, metal concentrations has 
generated considerable discussion in the literature (e.g., Birch et al., 
2000 ; Matschullat et al., 2000 ; Bindler et al., 2011 ; Geiselbrecht et al., 
2019 ). To obtain the likely upper limit on background values and better 
assess the degree of anthropogenic metal contamination, I used the 2 ϭ

__data__.text:
Geomorphology 426 (2023) 108603
4
method of Matschullat et al. (2000) . As outlined in my earlier work 
( Martin, 2004 ), I use deeply buried sediments to establish natural 
background metal concentrations in this study. Evidence that deeply- 
buried sediments are appropriate for establishing background concen -
trations comes from several AMS conventional radiocarbon ages on 
charcoal recovered from depths > 0.60 m along the Dill River ( Martin, 
2015 ). The radiocarbon ages indicate that sediments at those depths are 
pre-nineteenth century in age. 
In addition to comparing sample metal concentrations to those of 
background values, several published standards provide a means to 
evaluate the degree of soil contamination. Standards for assessing the 
degree of soil contamination in Germany are outlined in the German 
Federal Soil Protection Act of 1998 ( Bundes-Bodenschutzgesetz 
{BbodSchG} ) and the German Federal Soil Protection and Contaminated 
Sites Ordinance of 1999 ( Bundes-Bodenschutzverordnung {BbodSchV} ). 
Precautionary values (mg kg
� 1 
for dry weight fine soil), the value at 
which natural soil functions are said to be at risk, are outlined in the 
protection act and ordinance. Here, the metal concentrations from the 
2000, 2007, and 2019 samples were compared to the precautionary 
values as an additional measure of the degree of soil contamination. 
Finally, the threshold effect concentration (TEC) and probable effect 
concentration (PEC) guidelines developed by MacDonald et al. (2000) 
were compared to the 2000, 2007, and 2019 metal concentrations. 
Adverse effects are deemed “ unlikely ” when metal concentrations fall 
below the TEC. Concentrations above the PEC will likely have negative 
effects on the soil. 
4. Results 
4.1. Mean metal concentrations, 2007 and 2019 
The near-channel median concentrations of Cu and Zn were statis -
tically unchanged, whereas the concentration of Pb increased, between 
2007 and 2019 ( Table 1 ). Based on a Mann-Whitney U test comparison 
of median values, the increase in Pb concentration was statistically 
significant ( p = 0.03). Interestingly, the maximum values as reflected in 
the ranges for all three metals were greater in 2019 than in 2007, with

4.2. Spatial pattern of metal concentrations 
Examining the spatial pattern of changes in metal concentrations 
between 2007 and 2019 reveals that changes vary for different reaches 
of the study area. As was the case in 2000 and 2007 ( Martin, 2012 ), trace 
metals in 2019 increased in a downstream direction ( Fig. 2 ), but site-to- 
site variability for each trace metal continues to be evident. To examine 
the spatial variability of each trace metal across the sample dates, I 
divided the study area into three reaches in a downstream direction: 
Marburg to Giessen (Mb-Gi), Giessen to Wetzlar (Gi-Wz), and Wetzlar to

the Gi-Wz river reach.

which empties into the Lahn River in Wetzlar. The Dill River and Wz-Wb 
reach of the Lahn River drain areas that were extensively mined for iron 
from the late nineteenth century until the early 1980s. Martin (2015) 
documented that high concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn are stored in 
geomorphically-sensitive, near-channel locations along the Dill River, 
where they may be periodically conveyed downstream to the Lahn 
River. The source of the metals appears to be upstream industrial fa -
cilities in the Dill River, not the historic iron mining activity that 
occurred in the basin until the late twentieth century ( Martin, 2019 ). 
The 2019 data indicate that trace metal concentrations, although 
increasing overall in a downstream direction, are spatially variable from 
site to site. “ Hotspots ” with anomalously high concentrations may exist 
at one location, but immediately downstream at the next sample loca -
tion the concentrations are much lower. This complex, irregular spatial 
pattern was also apparent in the 2000 and 2007 samples and has been 
noted in other studies of trace metals in near-channel positions (e.g., 
Coulthard and Macklin, 2003 ; Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014 ). It is usually 
attributed to geomorphic processes that control storage and transport of 
metal-contaminated sediments ( Dhivert et al., 2016 ), differences in 
topographic relief ( Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2001 ; Middelkoop, 2002 ), or 
the presence of multiple sources of trace metals along a study reach 
( Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2014 ). In the study reach, there is little change in 
topographic relief in near-channel positions. Multiple potential sources 
of trace metals are found along the study reach, although the number of 
large point sources on or close to the floodplain (e.g., large industrial

metals continue to be transported through the upper Lahn River, prob -

4.3. Normalizing metal concentrations 
To evaluate the potential influence of substrate on metal concen -
trations, metal concentrations were normalized for Al, Fe, clay and OM 
(all reported in %). A general look at the differences in these variables 
between 2007 and 2019 is provided in Table 3 . Median clay and OM 
values between the two dates are not statistically different. Median 
values of Al and Fe were statistically lower in 2019 than in 2007, sug -
gesting a potential difference in substrate between the 2019 and 2007 
samples. The normalized concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn with Al and Fe 
for 2000, 2007 and 2019 are shown in Fig. 3 . Comparison of the 
normalized concentration trends with the original concentration trends 
( Fig. 2 ) reveals only minor changes at a handful of sites. At a few sites 
normalization with Fe or Al brings the values for the three years closer 
together, but at other sites normalization pulls the values apart. Overall, 
it appears that Al and Fe concentrations have little impact on metal 
concentration trends, suggesting that changes are a function of metal 
sources rather than of substrate. 
As an additional normalization of trace metal concentrations, I 
compared metal ratio median values for the 2007 and 2019 samples to 
gauge the impact of substrate on median metal concentrations for the 
two periods ( Table 4 ) and determine whether changes in metal con -
centrations are the result of increased metal input to the study reach or 
the result of changes in substrate. The three trace metals were normal -
ized for Al and Fe. The difference in mean and median ratio values for Cu 
and Zn for the two periods is small and statistically insignificant. In 
contrast, the mean and median ratio values for Pb are larger in 2019 
than in 2007, and the difference in the median ratio value is statistically 
higher in 2019 than in 2007. This suggests that the increase in Pb con -
centration over that period is a function of a higher input of Pb to the 
system rather than of changes in substrate. 
To gauge the impact of Al, Fe, clay, and organic matter more closely 
on the 2019 samples, I isolated the five sites in 2019 with the highest Cu, 
Pb, and Zn concentrations and the five sites with the lowest Cu, Pb, and 
Zn concentrations, then compared their Al, Fe, clay and OM values 
( Table 5 ). The maximum median values of Cu, Pb, and Zn are statisti -
cally different than the minimum median values at the sites, but there is 
no statistical difference in the median Fe (%), clay (%) and OM content 
(%) between the maximum and minimum sites. In contrast, the median 
Al (%) is statistically higher in the maximum sites than in the minimum 
sites. 
A series of bivariate regression plots ( Fig. 4 ) for the 2019 data depict 
the relationship between metal concentrations (Cu, Pb, and Zn) and Fe, 
Al, clay, and OM content (all reported in %). Cu concentrations have a

5. Discussion 
Returning to near-channel sites along the Lahn River that were 
sampled in 2000 and 2007, this study extends the record of change in 
trace metal concentrations to 2019 and provides an indication of the 
persistence of trace metal contamination along the Lahr River. For the 
75-km study reach, this study reveals no statistical change in Cu and Zn 
concentrations, but an increase in Pb concentrations. Although median 
concentrations of all three trace metals are statistically greater than 
median background concentrations in both 2007 and 2019, only Zn 
exceeds the 2 ϭ upper limit for background concentrations. This suggests 
that the study reach is not heavily contaminated with anthropogenic 
trace metals, not unexpected given the relatively agrarian character of 
the Lahn River drainage basin. Further evidence of the degree of 
anthropogenic trace metal concentration in the study reach comes from 
comparing the 2019 trace metal concentrations to other sediment 
quality guidelines such as the TEC and PEC of MacDonald et al. (2000) 
and the “ Precautionary Value ” of the German Federal Soil Protection Act 
of 1998. Such comparisons show that the study reach is not highly 
contaminated, but also reveal that Pb contamination worsened slightly 
between 2007 and 2019 whereas Cu and Zn contamination was virtually 
unchanged. 
The increased near-channel concentrations of Pb between 2007 and 
2019 noted in this study may result from the availability of the metal in 
the Lahn River basin and periodic conveyance of it to the river channel 
and near-channel positions. Previous work along five transects perpen -
dicular to the Lahn River ( Martin, 2009 ) revealed that Pb and Zn

present in soils and surface sediments across the floodplain. 
In addition to spatial variability in metal concentrations, temporal 
variability is captured in vertical metals trends from near-channel cores 
collected along the lower Lahn River ( Martin, 2019 ) and Dill River 
( Martin, 2015 ). They revealed that metal concentrations vary with 
depth and appear to reflect peak releases of metals to the environment 
from upstream industrial activity, mining, or both. Although site-to-site 
differences exist, the vertical metal trends in cores are similar. This 
suggests that vertical metal trends reflect changing metal inputs to the 
river rather than inherent variability in metal concentrations. At least 
over the short term covered in this study and my previous work 
stretching back to 2000, temporal declines in trace metal concentrations 
to European watersheds (e.g., Grosbois et al., 2006 ; Meybeck et al., 
2007 ; Le Gall et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2019 ) are not evident along this 
reach of the Lahn River. To the extent they represent the current 
geochemical load moving through the active channel ( Lecce et al., 
2008 ), the three “ grab samples ” collected from freshly-deposited 
sediments at a site near Giessen shortly after a flood in March 2019 
confirm that contaminated sediments are still being transported through 
the upper Lahn River. All three samples contain Cu, Pb, and Zn con -
centrations that exceed background levels. 
Metal concentrations in 2019 generally increase with distance 
downstream, with maximum concentrations present downstream from 
Wetzlar. The Dill River, which empties into the Lahn River at Wetzlar, is 
likely the source of the higher metal concentrations as near-channel 
positions along the Dill River store relatively high concentrations of 
trace metals ( Martin, 2015 ) that may be periodically conveyed to the 
Lahn River. Concealed within the general increase in metal concentra -
tions downstream, there is variability among river reaches that I high -
light by dividing the study reach into three river segments: Mb – Gi, 
Gi – Wz, and Wz – Wb. Mean Zn concentrations were greater than the 2 ϭ 
upper limit for background samples in all three segments in 2007 and 
2019, mean Cu concentrations exceed the 2 ϭ upper limit in one segment 
(Wz-Wb) in 2007 and 2019, and mean Pb concentrations were less than 
the upper limit in all three segments in 2007 and 2019. Using this in -
dicator, anthropogenic contamination with Zn is present along the entire 
study area, but contamination with Cu and Pb is less widespread. Mean 
concentrations of all three metals generally exceed the TEC baseline of 
MacDonald et al. (2000) in all three segments, but fall below the PEC 
baseline (the exception is Zn (2019) which is above the PEC value in the 
Wz-Wb reach. In summary, comparing the 2019 concentrations of Cu, 
Pb, and Zn with various background and baseline indicators reveals 
more anthropogenic contamination with Zn than with Cu and Pb, but 
evidence of at least minor anthropogenic storage of all three metals in 
near-channel positions, especially in the Wz-Wb river segment, is 
present.

sampling depth in all three dates was 5 cm, it is possible that the 5 cm 
samples in 2019 were from different sediment than the 5 cm samples 
collected in 2000 or 2007. Field evidence that would allow me to 
identify such sites is lacking, but the “ grab samples ” noted in this study 
were collected from single-event flood deposits that were ~ 1.5 cm 
thick, so ≥ 5 cm of sedimentation between 2000 and 2019 is reasonable. 
As shown in Figs. 2 and 3 , temporal variation in metal concentrations 
(both original and normalized) among the three sample dates is greatest 
for Cu and Zn in the Gi-Wz river section, whereas there is little difference 
in the temporal variation for Pb across the three river sections. If the 
differences in metal concentrations for Cu and Zn in the Gi-Wz section 
are caused by samples being collected from different sediments in 2000, 
2007, and 2019, one would expect the temporal variation for Pb to also 
be at a maximum in that reach. The fact that it is not suggests that 
different sedimentation rates do not play a major role in explaining 
metal concentrations among the three sample dates. Additionally, if 
sedimentation rates were a major factor in accounting for differences 
among the 2000, 2007 and 2019 samples, one would expect more 
consistent changes at given sites for all three metals over the three time 
periods. For example, if the addition of new sediment at a given site 
sometime between 2000 and 2019 was an important factor, then the 
2019 values for Cu, Pb, and Zn should all be either greater, roughly 
equal to, or less than the 2000 values. In fact, for many individual sites 
the 2019 Pb value is clearly greater than the 2000 and 2007 Pb values, 
but the 2019 Cu and Zn values are equal to or less than the 2000 and 
2007 values. As noted earlier, on a sample site basis, the Cu and Zn 
concentrations increased at 16 and 15 sites, respectively, between 2007 
and 2019, whereas the Pb concentration increased at 23 sites during the 
same time period. If sedimentation between 2007 and 2019 was 
impacting changes in metal concentrations, the number of sites where 
the concentrations increased should be roughly equal for all the three 
metals. Additional inputs of Pb to the study reach between 2007 and 
2019 are a more plausible explanation for Pb concentrations increasing 
at more sites than did Cu or Zn concentrations. 
Linked to a potential spatial variation in sedimentation between 
2007 and 2019 is the possibility that some parts of the study reach 
experienced overbank flows whereas other parts did not. In this sce -
nario, those areas that were flooded would have received inputs of new 
sediments that would then have been sampled in 2019, or alternatively 
experienced erosion of the floodplain surface that removed the sedi -
ments sampled in 2007. Arguing against erosion of the floodplain sur -
face is the thick vegetation cover present in a several-meter wide near- 
channel buffer zone on both sides of the Lahn River throughout nearly 
all of the study reach. In addition, overbank flow in the study reach tends 
to be low velocity given the gentle gradient of the river (0.02

Lahn River during the mid-1800s to facilitate navigation reduce river 
and overbank velocity. In many years of work along the Lahn River 
before, during, and after high water events, I have never observed sig -
nificant near-channel soil/surface sediment erosion.

Arguing against erosion of the floodplain sur -
face is the thick vegetation cover present in a several-meter wide near- 
channel buffer zone on both sides of the Lahn River throughout nearly 
all of the study reach. In addition, overbank flow in the study reach tends 
to be low velocity given the gentle gradient of the river (0.02
◦
- 0.14
◦
) 
throughout the study reach. Finally, numerous step-dams built in the 
Lahn River during the mid-1800s to facilitate navigation reduce river 
and overbank velocity. In many years of work along the Lahn River 
before, during, and after high water events, I have never observed sig -
nificant near-channel soil/surface sediment erosion. Rather, vertical 
accretion such as documented in March 2019 and sampled at that time is 
far more common. Documenting the size, timing, and frequency of 
overbank flows in the study reach is complicated by the fact that the 
closest gauging station to the study reach is located in Dietz, about 35 
km downstream from the end of the study reach. In addition, collection 
of discharge data began on 1 January 2012. Thus, the temporal and 
spatial resolution of the discharge data provides little information on 
overbank events that might have impacted the study reach between 
2000 and 2019. 
Nonetheless, it is possible that overbank flow events between 2007 
and 2019 differentially impacted the study reach and played a role in the 
observed changes in metal concentrations over that period. But as was 
noted above in the discussion of differences in sedimentation rates, one 
would expect sites that received new sediment to show a consistent 
difference in concentrations for all three metals when comparing 2000, 
2007 and 2019 data. As previously stated, if sediment events between 
2000 and 2019 were impacting changes in metal concentrations, the 
number of sites where the concentrations increased should be roughly 
equal for the three metals. In fact, they are not as detailed above. The 
complex spatial pattern of metal concentrations is as apparent in the 
2019 data as it was in the 2000 and 2007 data. “ Hotspots ” with anom -
alously high metal concentrations are scattered through the 75-km study 
reach; Martin (2015) found a similar spatial pattern in near-channel 
locations along the nearby Dill River. The spatial patterns could be 
related to geomorphic processes ( Dhivert et al., 2016 ) that operate over 
small spatial scales to create a variable pattern of metal deposition and 
storage, although that would require processes operating differently on 
Pb than on Cu and Zn. Differences in topography (e.g., floodplain swales 
vs. point bars), another factor that has been shown to impact metal 
storage ( Lecce and Pavlowsky, 2001 ; Szab ´o et al., 2020 ), is another 
possible explanatory factor, but again that would require that topog -
raphy is affecting accumulation of Cu and Zn differently than accumu -
lation of Pb. My previous work along transects perpendicular to the Lahn 
River has revealed no differences in metal concentrations between 
swales and flatter areas of the floodplain ( Martin, 2009 ). The different 
spatial variability of Cu/Zn in contrast to Pb may reflect multiple sources 
for the latter metal in the study area, as noted by Lecce and Pavlowsky 
(2014) . Multiple sources for Pb have resulted in a more even distribution 
of the metal (that is, less site-to-site lateral and downstream variability) 
in the study reach. 
6. Conclusion 
Concentrations of Cu and Zn at near-channel positions along the 
Lahn River, central Germany, were unchanged between 2007 and 2019; 
in contrast, the concentration of Pb increased over the period. The Cu 
and Zn concentrations increased at 48 % and 45 %, respectively, of the 
33 sample sites between 2007 and 2019. In contrast, Pb concentrations 
increased at 70 % of the sample sites over the study period.

6. Conclusion 
Concentrations of Cu and Zn at near-channel positions along the 
Lahn River, central Germany, were unchanged between 2007 and 2019; 
in contrast, the concentration of Pb increased over the period. The Cu 
and Zn concentrations increased at 48 % and 45 %, respectively, of the 
33 sample sites between 2007 and 2019. In contrast, Pb concentrations 
increased at 70 % of the sample sites over the study period. When the 
study reach is divided into three river segments, Cu, Pb, and Zn median 
and mean concentrations increased in the Mb-Gi and Wz-Wb sections 
between 2007 and 2019; in the third section (Gi-Wz), mean and median 
concentrations of Cu and Zn and the median concentration of Pb 
decreased whereas the mean concentration of Pb increased. The median 
concentrations of all three metals are statistically higher than back -
ground values, but only Zn concentrations exceed the 2 ϭ background 
upper limit. The most downstream segment of the study reach (Wz-Wb) 
continued to have the highest concentrations of all three trace metals. 
The spatial pattern downstream of metal concentrations remains 
variable. Individual near-channel sites with relatively high metal con -
centrations, sometimes referred to as “ hotspots ” , continue to appear in 
the 2019 samples. Although I cannot identify the exact mechanism that 
results in such hotspots, their existence appears to be independent of 
factors such as differences in substrate, inherent non-anthropogenic 
spatial variability in metal concentrations, variable sedimentation 
rates and flood history, and clay and organic matter content. Rather, the 
existence of sites with high metal contents suggests that input of metals 
to the river system continues. That is, they reflect source inputs rather 
than other factors. Locations with higher metal concentrations also 
represent problematic potential sources for downstream metal pollution 
into the future. Indeed, they may already be serving as sources, along 
with former mining activity, for metal pollution noted in reaches of the 
Lahn River downstream from the study reach ( Hahn et al., 2021 ). 
Increasing Pb concentrations in near-channel sediments along most 
of the entire study reach suggests a reversal from previous years in the 
conveyance of Pb-contaminated sediments through the river. At least 
between 2007 and 2019, cleaner sediments were not being deposited in 
near-channel positions. It is possible that “ saturation ” , or the storage of

Pb in upstream soils and sediments ( Nriagu et al., 1998 ; Outridge et al., 
2011 ), is producing a lag between the decline in metal emissions to the 
environment and the decrease in metal concentrations in downstream 
depositional environments. Indeed, in the case of Pb throughout the 
study reach, and Cu and Zn in a large part of it, the reduction in metal 
emissions to the environment is currently not resulting in decreasing 
metal concentrations moving through, and being deposited along, the 
Lahn River. Between 2007 and 2019, near channel metal concentrations 
appear to have become “ uncoupled ” from the trend in metal releases to 
the environment. An increase in Cu, Pb, and Zn emissions to the envi -
ronment between 2007 and 2019 is possible, but unlikely given the 
prevalence of strict environmental controls in Germany. It is more likely 
that the river, or surface water systems flowing into the river, are 
conveying more metal-rich sediments downstream. Surface soils, and 
sub-surface sediments of channel banks along the Lahn River, have been 
shown to contain concentrations of all three trace metals that exceed 
background values ( Martin, 2004 ), with maximum metal concentrations 
found either at the surface or just below it ( Martin, 2019 ). Additionally, 
relatively high concentrations of Pb are present in soils and surface 
sediments laterally across the Lahn River floodplain ( Martin, 2009 ). 
Higher-than-background concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn are also 
present just below the surface at near-channel locations along the Dill 
River ( Martin, 2015 ), which enters the Lahn River at Wetzlar. 
A limited picture of the metal concentrations currently being 
conveyed through the Lahn River is provided by the three “ grab ” sam -
ples collected from freshly deposited flood silts. All three samples con -
tained concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn that are above background 
concentrations, an indication that anthropogenic metals continue to be 
transported through the Lahn River by flood events. The results from the 
“ grab ” samples demonstrate that upstream locations remain sources for 
anthropogenic metal contamination in the study reach. Simply, metal 
concentrations equal to or less than background levels are not presently 
being conveyed through the river system. Rather, elevated concentra -
tions of trace metals persist in near-channel positions of the Lahn River 
study reach. Reducing heavy metal concentrations stored in channel 
banks of the river could be a lengthy process that will lag behind the 
already-realized reductions in metals to the environment and may 
periodically involve reversals in metal trends, as appears to have 
happened here with Pb concentrations between 2007 and 2019.

ORIGINAL ARTICLE
Recent changes in heavy metal storage in ﬂood-plain soils
of the Lahn River, central Germany
Charles W. Martin
Received: 3 June 2008 / Accepted: 16 September 2008 / Published online: 2 October 2008
/C211Springer-Verlag 2008
Abstract Between 1995 and 2007, the concentrations of
Pb and Zn in ﬂoodplain soils increased along a 60-km
reach of the Lahn River, Germany, suggesting that the
storage of some metals in the ﬂuvial system is out of phase
with recent declines in the release of metals to the envi-
ronment. Re-sampling of surface soils to 5 cm along ﬁve
transects perpendicular to the river indicated that the con-
centration of Pb increased between 1995 and 2007 along
two transects and was statistically unchanged at the other
three. The concentration of Zn increased at three of ﬁve
transects and was statistically unchanged at two transects
over the same time period. Between 1995 and 2007, con-
centrations of Cu were statistically equal along four of ﬁve
transects and declined at the other transect. The increase in
Pb and Zn was greater in a more rural than in a more
urbanized reach of the Lahn River. Soil texture and organic
matter content had virtually no impact on the concentration
of metals. The increase in Pb concentration suggests a lag
between the decline in Pb releases to the environment and
its movement through the ﬂuvial system. Increased Zn
storage may result from the high solubility of the metal and
the relative ease with which it moves through the envi-
ronment. Environmental controls appear to have slowed Cu
storage along the Lahn River, but are not yet reﬂected in Pb
and Zn storage.
Keywords Heavy metals /C1Floodplain metal storage /C1
Recent environmental contamination /C1Germany
Introduction
In densely populated, highly industrialized Western Eur-
ope, there is a long history of pollution being delivered to
and conveyed through ﬂuvial systems. In the watersheds of
Germany, arguably the most industrialized nation in
Western Europe, heavy metals are among the most studied
pollutants. Years before re-uniﬁcation, the former West
Germany began enacting meaningful controls on the dis-
charge of pollutants, including heavy metals, to its surface
water systems. Since the end of the Cold War and re-uni-
ﬁcation of the country, the spread of pollutants from
Eastern Europe, whether by air or water, has also been
reduced. In spite of considerable effort, rivers in Germany
reﬂect the legacy of centuries of exposure to anthropogenic
pollutants. Heavy metals, usually the product of industrial
or mining activity, have been discharged to the environ-
ment for centuries (Matschullat et al. 1997; Bra¨ nnvall et al.
1999; Renberg et al. 2001), with the greatest releases
occurring from the mid-1800s until the early 1970s
(Valette-Silver 1993; Middelkoop 2002). The release of
metals to the environment dropped substantially beginning
in the early 1970s (Matschullat and Bozau 1996; Schulte
et al. 1996;D a¨ mmgen et al. 2000; Scherer et al. 2003;
Zerling et al. 2006). The decline accelerated in the early
1990s following the closing of many aged industrial
facilities and the installation of modern industrial waste-
water treatment facilities in the countries of Eastern Europe
(Scherer et al. 2003; Zerling et al. 2006).
Although surface water systems in Germany have
become markedly cleaner over the last few decades, large
stores of heavy metals remain along rivers.

__data__.text:
(Fo¨ rstner 2003; Kru¨ ger et al. 2005; Schwartz et al. 2006).
Because of their potential to transport large quantities of
heavy metals, rivers in industrial or mined areas of
Germany and the Netherlands have received the bulk of
attention from researchers. Much, for example, is known
about heavy metal pollution in the Elbe River (Bru ¨ gmann
1995;F o¨ rstner 2003; Kru¨ ger and Gro¨ ngro¨ ft 2003; Kru¨ ger
et al. 2005; Schwartz et al. 2006) and the Rhine River
(Dehner 1994; Middelkoop 2002; Wijnhoven et al. 2006).
When stored in ﬂoodplain soils or sediments, metals
pose little threat to the environment. Concerns arise when
they become mobile. The mobility of heavy metals is
inﬂuenced by parameters such as pH, redox potential,
atmospheric oxygen, and the concentration of complexing
agents (Zehl and Einax 2005). In doing a risk assessment of
metals stored in a particular environment, it is important to
ascertain the bioavilability of metals and their potential
uptake by biota (Wijnhoven et al. 2006). Heavy metals
stored along rivers and streams may also re-enter the
environment through erosion. Geomorphically active
locations (e.g., channel banks, near-channel ﬂoodplains,
frequently-ﬂooded low elevation surfaces) have the
potential of serving as signiﬁcant sources of heavy metal
pollution (James 1989; Marcus 1989; Leigh 1997; Leece
and Pavlowsky 2001). In contrast, those surfaces that are
geomorphically ‘‘quiet’’ (e.g., infrequently ﬂooded sur-
faces, distal ﬂoodplains, surfaces protected by levees/high
channel banks) may store metals for decades or longer
(Foster and Charlesworth 1996; Zhao et al. 1999; Coult-
hard and Macklin 2003). Locally, channel bank erosion
reduces heavy metal concentrations, and thus the risk to
biota, but elevates the risk of contamination downstream
(Schwartz et al. 2006).
Understandably, most research in Germany has focused
on large drainage basins in industrial or mined areas
(e.g., Bru¨ gmann 1995;F o¨ rstner 2003; Schwartz et al.
2006). Less is known about heavy metal pollution in more
rural watersheds. Since the mid-1990s the storage and
distribution of heavy metals in the Lahn River basin of
central Germany had been the focus of my research (Martin
1997, 2000, 2004). A relatively rural watershed, the Lahn
River drains an area of approximately 5,000 km 2 at its
mouth in the Rhine River south of Koblenz (Fig. 1). Not
surprisingly, the aggregate storage of heavy metals (Cu, Pb,
Zn) along the Lahn River is less than that noted along
waterways such as the Rhine or Elbe, although there are
individual sites where metal concentrations approach levels
usually found in urbanized watersheds (Martin 2004).
Laterally, heavy metal concentrations are at a maximum in
near-channel sediments ( \100 m from active channel),
suggesting that the metals are a ﬂuvial rather than an eolian
deposit (Martin 2000). Vertically, the largest stores of
metals are found in the upper 15 cm of the ﬂoodplain.
Below depths of 25 cm the concentrations are virtually
identical to concentrations in deeply buried sediments
(Martin 1997, 2000). At most sites along the Lahn River,
surface samples contain lower concentrations of heavy
metals than samples collected between 15 and 20 cm
below the surface, evidence of the decline in metal releases
to the environment since the early 1970s (Bru¨ gmann 1995;
Middelkoop 2002; Zerling et al. 2006).

Laterally, heavy metal concentrations are at a maximum in
near-channel sediments ( \100 m from active channel),
suggesting that the metals are a ﬂuvial rather than an eolian
deposit (Martin 2000). Vertically, the largest stores of
metals are found in the upper 15 cm of the ﬂoodplain.
Below depths of 25 cm the concentrations are virtually
identical to concentrations in deeply buried sediments
(Martin 1997, 2000). At most sites along the Lahn River,
surface samples contain lower concentrations of heavy
metals than samples collected between 15 and 20 cm
below the surface, evidence of the decline in metal releases
to the environment since the early 1970s (Bru¨ gmann 1995;
Middelkoop 2002; Zerling et al. 2006).
The present study was undertaken to assess recent
changes in heavy metal concentrations along a 60-km reach
of the Lahn River between Marburg and Wetzlar. Samples
were collected from 50 sites along ﬁve transects that had
been sampled in 1994 and 1995 (Martin 1997). In addition,
the geographic coordinates of sample sites were recorded
using a hand-held GPS unit in order to permit future
monitoring of heavy metal storage. The objectives of the
study are to (1) ascertain whether the concentration of
heavy metals at the 50 sites has changed since 1994/1995,
(2) look at the geographic pattern of any changes in metal
concentrations along the transects, and (3) evaluate the
effect of organic matter content, grain size, and distance
from the active channel on heavy metal concentrations and
determine whether changes occurred since the earlier
samples were collected. By updating the inventory of
heavy metal concentrations begun over a decade ago, this
study provides a picture of short-term change in heavy
metal storage along part of a rural river system and
examines how metals travel through a watershed over time.
The ﬁndings may also be useful in gauging the effective-
ness of environmental controls that have reduced the
emission of heavy metals to the environment since the
early 1970s.
Study area
From headwaters in the rural uplands north of Marburg,
the Lahn River ﬂows southward through a broad valley
between Marburg and Giessen, then turns westward
towards Wetzlar. The ﬂoodplain for nearly all of the study
area is wide, reaching a maximum width of about 2.5 km
just downriver of Giessen. The watershed is 70% agri-
cultural land, 16% forested land, and 14% urban land
(Jo¨ ckel 1981), a stark contrast to the more urban water-
sheds that have been the focus of most research on heavy
metal storage in Germany and adjacent countries. The
ﬂoodplain of the Lahn River is cultivated or grazed,
whereas uplands remain largely forested. Downstream
from Giessen the Lahn River watershed becomes pro-
gressively more urbanized. At the downstream end of the
study area is Wetzlar, well-known for its optical industry,
but also an historical center of heavy industry (e.g.,
smelting, steel).

__data__.text:
As a consequence of channelization in the mid-1800s,
ﬂow of the river is sluggish for much of the year, although
higher precipitation and snowmelt often increase discharge
during the winter. Overbank ﬂow for a week or two is
common between January and March, eroding the channel
locally and depositing ﬁne sands on point bars and near-
channel surfaces. Examination of aerial photographs taken
between 1935 and 1995, coupled with considerable ﬁeld
experience in the Lahn River basin since 1995, indicate
that most reaches of the channel have been stable for some
time. The presence of meander scars in the study reach
suggests, however, that historical lateral migration was
common (Martin, 2000). Between Marburg and Wetzlar,
the Lahn River ﬂows in late Holocene alluvium. The
ﬂoodplain of the Lahn River is underlain by black, organic-
rich silt that accumulated over the last 1,000 years (Ma¨ ckel
1969; Houben 2003), presumably as a result of erosion on
surrounding hillslopes when they were cleared of forest
cover for agriculture and timber (Rittweger 2000; Kalis
et al. 2003; Rommens et al. 2006; Hoffmann et al. 2007). In
the vicinity of the Lahn River, this black silt reaches a
thickness of up to 2 m (Bos and Urz 2003; Houben 2003;
Kalis et al. 2003). Soils typically have an A/AC/C proﬁle, a
mean pH of 5.2, and a clayey silt texture.
Methods
Field notes, topographic maps, and ground-based photog-
raphy were used to relocate the ﬁve transects and 50
sample sites from 1994 and 1995. Because it is channelized
and ﬂow tends to be fairly sluggish, the channel of the
Lahn River remained stable between 1994 and 2007. Land
use in the study area also changed little since the initial
sampling. Likewise, no new transportation routes were
built in the study reach and suburban sprawl, a rarity in
Germany because of strict zoning regulations, was mini-
mal. In short, the physical and human environment of the
study area changed little between 1994 and 2007.
Working along transects, cores were extracted to a depth
of 5 cm from the same sites where samples had been col-
lected in previous work. Samples were relocated based on

River between Marburg and
Wetzlar, Germany. Study
transects are: D Dorlar, G
Garbenheim, H Heuchelheim,
R Roth, S Sichertshausen

__data__.text:
ﬁeld notes and ﬁeld measurements made with a surveyor’s
tape in 1994 and 1995. Samples in 1994/1995 and 2007
were positioned across the ﬂoodplain at a systematic
interval measured from the active channel of the Lahn
River. The sampling interval along transects ranged from
25 to 100 m, depending on ﬂoodplain width (Martin 1997).
At locations where the Lahn valley was wide (e.g., Heu-
chelheim), the interval was 100 m; where the valley was
narrower (e.g., Dorlar), the interval was 25 m. Samples
were stored in sterile plastic bags for transport to the
geomorphology lab at Justus Liebig-Universita¨ t in Giessen.
The latitude and longitude of each sample location were
recorded using a hand-held GPS unit. Location accuracy as
reported on the GPS was 4–7 m.
Once in the lab, samples were split, with half submitted
to ALS Chemex Labs, an ISO 9002 registered analytical
laboratory in North America, for analysis of heavy metals,
and the other half retained for standard soil analyses. To
ensure comparability of samples collected in 1994/1995
and 2007, samples were submitted to the same ALS Che-
mex facility in North Vancouver, Canada, used in previous
work and identical laboratory preparation procedures (air
drying of samples, screening to 63 lm) were followed.
Samples were digested in perchloric, nitric, and hydroﬂu-
oric acids (triple-acid digestion), a process that yields near
total recovery of metals (Leece and Pavlowsky 1997).
Concentrations of Cu, Pb, and Zn were then determined by
inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy
(ICP-AES); the concentrations of Cd were also measured,
but the results are omitted because the analytical capabil-
ities for Cd (0.5 mg kg
-1) differ little from the Cd
concentrations found in surface soils in earlier work
(Martin 2000, 2004). Concentrations were measured in mg/
kg with an analytical sensitivity of 1.0 mg kg -1 for Cu,
and 2.0 mg kg -1 for Pb and Zn. According to Quality
Control data supplied by ALS Chemex, repeated mea-
surement of standards produced coefﬁcients of variation of
1% for Cu, 5% for Pb, and 3.5% for Zn. Analysis of
duplicates yielded a mean difference of 1.25 mg kg
-1 for
Cu, 0.75 mg kg -1 for Pb, and 5.8 mg kg -1 for Zn, with
coefﬁcients of variation \4% for all three metals. The
coefﬁcients of variation for standards and duplicates noted
here are similar to those reported by Leece et al. ( 2008) for
samples analyzed for heavy metals by ALS Chemex. In the
geomorphic lab at Justus Liebig-Universita ¨ t, the propor-
tions of clay (\2 lm) and silt (2–63 lm) were determined
on the other half of each sample using the pipette method;
the sand percentage was measured through wet sieving.
Organic matter content was measured by loss on ignition
(LOI) at 430 /C176C for 24 h (Davies 1974). These analyses
were carried out by the author.
The surface samples were also compared to background
samples to evaluate the degree of anthropogenic enrichment.
Background values, which represent pre-industrial age
(pre-1750 AD) metal concentrations, were obtained from
deeply buried sediments (0.85–1.15 m) collected within
5 m of the Lahn River channel. As noted by Martin ( 2004),
ascertaining non-anthropogenic, or background, metal
concentrations is problematic, but sediments collected at a
depth of ca. 1 m in the study area can be assumed to reﬂect
pre-industrial concentrations of metals (Martin 2000).

Organic matter content was measured by loss on ignition
(LOI) at 430 /C176C for 24 h (Davies 1974). These analyses
were carried out by the author.
The surface samples were also compared to background
samples to evaluate the degree of anthropogenic enrichment.
Background values, which represent pre-industrial age
(pre-1750 AD) metal concentrations, were obtained from
deeply buried sediments (0.85–1.15 m) collected within
5 m of the Lahn River channel. As noted by Martin ( 2004),
ascertaining non-anthropogenic, or background, metal
concentrations is problematic, but sediments collected at a
depth of ca. 1 m in the study area can be assumed to reﬂect
pre-industrial concentrations of metals (Martin 2000).
Metal concentrations were compared to standards con-
tained in the German Federal Soil Protection Act ( Bundes-
Bodenschutzgesetz [BbodSchG] of 1998 and the German
Federal Soil Protection and Contaminated Sites Ordinance
(Bundes-Bodenschutzverordnung [BbodSchV] of 1999.
These federal acts set standards for various contaminants
above which some remediation action is required. When a
‘‘precautionary value’’ is exceeded, the natural soil func-
tions are said to be at risk. A higher level of concern is
attached to the ‘‘trigger value’’. It represents a concentra-
tion above which an investigation of the soil should be
undertaken to evaluate the extent and magnitude of the
contamination.
Results
Given the post-1989 reduction in metal releases to the
environment, the lack of a broad decline in heavy metal
storage in the study reach between 1994/1995 and 2007 is
surprising (Table 1). For Cu, the mean concentration in the
2007 samples (27.4 mg kg
-1) was not signiﬁcantly dif-
ferent than the concentration in 1994/1995 (28.8 mg kg -1).
The concentration of Cu in 2007 was higher at 22 sites
